job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Hassan Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in machine learning in Toronto and living in a shared flat near campus. My day starts with coffee and an AI coding assistant open next to my editor, then lectures, then a few hours on a side project: an inventory app for my family's restaurant on Dundas Street. My internship last summer was at a small health-tech start-up, where I wrote data pipelines. At night I cook for my flatmates, mostly my grandmother's lentil soup, and talk about whatever news is breaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say meh, I've used these tools every day for two years and they're good but not magic. In my class chat I'd say it's a nice speed-up for boilerplate and that's all. Online I'd post a thread about what actually works, because hype annoys me more than doom does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing dramatic for me. I'm already ahead of most people on the tools, the restaurant app brings in a bit of money, and there's a lot of hiring for engineers who can build with these models. A plateau actually helps my kind of skill because the tools stay assistants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep the restaurant app growing and apply for ML engineer roles. I'd try to sell the app to two other restaurants this winter, charge a small monthly fee and see if it grows. I'd put some savings in an index fund and leave the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, a bit like a free pass. I like change, but I don't need it to be huge for my own life to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the plateau means for ordinary workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot of change, which is both good and bad. It's good because jobs stay, bad because the boring parts of jobs stay too. My uncle, who works nights at the airport, still has the same schedule and the same bad back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that'd make you uneasy in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe stagnation. If nothing improves, there's less demand for new ideas and I'd be building into a flat market. But I'd still rather have a flat market than a collapsing one.

say: I'd say these tools are a **nice speed-up**, not magic, and hype annoys me more than doom.
I'd post a thread about what **actually works** in daily use.
think: A plateau suits my skills because the tools stay **assistants** and ML engineers stay in demand.
My restaurant **app** already brings in a little money.
do: Finish the master's and apply for **ML engineer** roles.
Sell the restaurant app to **two more** restaurants this winter for a small monthly fee.
feel: I feel **good**, like a free pass, though I like change and don't need it to be huge.
S0.quote: I'd still rather have a flat market than a collapsing one.
fieldNote: Hassan is **fluent** with the tools and treats a plateau as a safe, even comfortable world.
His side project makes him comfortable with risk and a bit entrepreneurial.
He worries only about **stagnation**, not job loss.

steps.text: Finish the master's and apply for machine learning engineer roles
Sell the restaurant inventory app to two more restaurants this winter
Put some savings into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should shape this, not just watch it. At school and online I'd argue for public AI tools and for unions to bargain over how firms use them, because the gains shouldn't go to five companies. I'd also teach friends how to use the tools well, since I know them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my skills are in the sweet spot. Entry-level coding jobs shrink, but the people who can build and supervise these systems get more valuable. I won't pretend there's zero risk, because a lot of juniors I know have stopped getting interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the restaurant app into a proper product with AI ordering and forecasting, and I'd launch it in the spring. I'd apply for roles at companies that build the models, not just companies that use them. I'd also run a free workshop for friends who are scared about this, once a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and a bit uncomfortable. I'm riding the wave, but I can see people drowning around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the friends you're most worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Dana (a classmate) who studied English and now writes product descriptions for an online shop. Her work is exactly what the models do well. I've offered to teach her prompt writing, but she also needs a union and a plan, not only a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the 'unions' point mean in practice for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want tech workers to unionise too. Programmers think they're special and can negotiate alone, but a thousand-person firm laying off a hundred coders in an afternoon shows they can't. I'd join one the day it exists.

say: I'd argue for **public AI tools** and for unions to bargain over how firms use it.
I'd teach friends to use the tools **well** because I know them.
think: My skills are in the **sweet spot**, since people who build and supervise these systems get more valuable.
Many **juniors** I know have stopped getting interviews.
do: Turn the restaurant app into a proper **product** with AI forecasting and launch it in spring.
Run a monthly free **workshop** for friends scared about this.
feel: I feel **excited** and a bit uncomfortable, riding the wave while others drown.
S1.quote: Programmers think they're special and can negotiate alone, but a thousand-person firm laying off a hundred coders in an afternoon shows they can't.
fieldNote: Hassan's optimism is real but **guilt-tinged**; he sees peers who are not as lucky.
He pairs entrepreneurship with a progressive demand for unions and public tools.
His help for others is practical and personal: workshops for friends.

steps.text: Launch the restaurant app with AI forecasting by spring
Run a free monthly AI workshop for worried friends
Join a tech workers' union as soon as one exists
Apply to firms that build the AI models themselves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is wild. I'd say loudly that governments need an emergency plan: income support, retraining and public ownership of at least some of the models. In my class chat I'd say don't freeze, move, build your own thing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm nervous. If AI can do almost any thinking job in 2028, the ML engineer roles I'm training for could shrink too, even though they're closest to the fire. I'd be 26 and my edge is just being early, which doesn't last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up the app and make it a small company before graduation, with two co-founders I trust. I'd stay close to the restaurants and tradespeople, because their work is hands-on and the robots come around 2031. I'd also put my savings in a safe account and ask my parents to hold off on the restaurant's expansion loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels dizzying. Exciting and frightening at once, and I can't say which wins on any given day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mother to keep the restaurant lean and not take on new debt. The customers still want food, so the kitchen is fine, but the paperwork and bookings change fast. I'd set up the booking and ordering software for them myself over a weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company doesn't work out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have learned a lot in a year and I still have family backing, which I'm lucky to have. But I'd also be in a world where lots of people have no backing at all, and I keep thinking about them.

say: I'd say governments need an **emergency plan** with income support, retraining and some public ownership.
I'd tell classmates **don't freeze**, build your own thing now.
think: Even the **ML engineer** roles I'm training for could shrink, since being early won't last.
I'm lucky to have **family backing**, and many people have none.
do: Turn the app into a **small company** before graduating with two co-founders.
Set up **booking and ordering** software for my family's restaurant in a weekend.
feel: I feel **dizzy**, excited and frightened at once.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mother to keep the restaurant lean and not take on new debt.
fieldNote: Hassan is **uneasy**, not panicked: he expects to be hit later than juniors and has a fallback.
His first move is to protect his family's restaurant from debt.
He keeps returning to people without backing.

steps.text: Form a small company around the app before graduation
Set up online booking and ordering software for the family restaurant
Move my savings into a safe account
Ask my mother to avoid new restaurant debt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I'd call a strong window. I'd say publicly that we should write the rules now, while the stakes are still abstract. I'd tell friends to learn the tools hard for two years, then decide what to specialise in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel fairly good. By 2031 I'd be 29, with five years of work and maybe a company. The thinking work goes, but people who understand how these systems fail will be needed, and I'd be one of them. I'd be sad for friends with less of a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at a model-building firm for two years to learn what's inside, then use that to build a company around trust and safety checks. I'd keep saving, put some into index funds, and help my parents add online ordering to the restaurant. I'd also keep running the monthly workshop for friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, actually. Five years is enough to plan, and I do like planning more than I admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you had the full ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd relax. Ten years means I could go slowly, take a doctorate, maybe a year abroad. Five means I choose the fastest route to a real income, and the first job matters more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part that still keeps you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap between people like me and people who have no one to teach them the tools. If the change only helps those who already have a head start, I'd be part of something I don't like.

I'd tell friends to learn the tools **hard** for two years, then specialise.
think: By 2031 people who understand how these systems **fail** will be needed, and I'd be one.
I'd be sad for friends with less of a **head start**.
do: Work two years at a **model-building** firm, then build a company around trust and safety checks.
Add **online ordering** to my parents' restaurant and keep the monthly workshop.
feel: I feel **okay**, because five years is enough to plan.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to plan, and I do like planning more than I admit.
fieldNote: Hassan's calm comes from a plan and from **early skill**.
His discomfort is moral, about the gap between the head-started and everyone else.
He separates the five-year route (fast income) from a slower ten-year route.

steps.text: Work two years at a model-building firm to learn how it works
Start a trust and safety checking company with colleagues
Add online ordering to the family restaurant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is generous. I'd say let's use it to build public institutions that share the gains: a basic income pilot, open models, training funds. I'd push for it online, because ten years is exactly how long these things take to pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm relaxed. In 2036 I'd be 34, likely running my own firm or working in public-interest tech. The hands-on robots come around 2039, which is a long time off for my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time PhD while working, and I'd run a small, honest company that builds tools for small restaurants and shops. I'd travel for a year before I'm 30 and I'd spend more time with my grandmother. I'd save normally and not stress about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels light. For once, the big thing is far enough away to enjoy the present.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's decided to ignore it all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say enjoy your twenties, but keep one skill in your pocket that you'd happily be paid for in ten years. Doesn't have to be code. It could be repairing bikes or teaching swimming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's 78 and she asks if a machine can read her prescriptions, because her eyes are bad. I'd love that world, honestly. Ten years gives time to make it work for her.

say: I'd say let's use the decade to build **public institutions** that share the gains.
I'd push for a **basic income pilot** and open models online.
think: In 2036 I'd be 34, likely running my own **firm** or in public-interest tech.
The hands-on **robots** around 2039 feel far from my career.
do: Do a part-time **PhD** while working and run a small honest company for restaurants and shops.
Spend a year **travelling** before 30 and more time with my grandmother.
feel: I feel **light**, because the big thing is far enough away to enjoy the present.
S4.quote: Keep one skill in your pocket that you'd happily be paid for in ten years. Doesn't have to be code.
fieldNote: Hassan's optimism is at its fullest here, with **time** for both ambition and family.
He ties technology to concrete good: reading prescriptions for his grandmother.
He wants everyone to keep one skill that isn't screen work.

steps.text: Study for a part-time PhD while working
Run a small tool company for local restaurants and shops
Campaign for a basic income pilot and open models

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because lots of friends wouldn't have time to react. What would help is an income floor, free retraining and open models anyone can use. I'm lucky, and I think a lot about how to share that luck.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people assume ML students are the winners. We might be early, but not safe, and I'd like that said out loud.

headlineQuote: We might be early, but not safe, and I'd like that said out loud.
portrait: Hassan is 24, doing a **machine learning** master's in Toronto and using AI tools every day.
He runs a small inventory app for his family's restaurant and sees **building** as his best protection.
He is progressive and wants unions, public models and an **income floor**.
In the fast scenario he is uneasy but acts quickly and stays close to family.
In slower worlds he is calm, plans a PhD and company, and thinks about people with **less backing**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because many friends would have no time to react.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor**, free retraining and open models anyone can use.
